**1 Corinthians 1**

 *Paul called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother,*

*2 Unto the church of God which is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, both their's and our's:*

*3 Grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ.*

*4 I thank my God always on your behalf, for the grace of God which is given you by Jesus Christ;*

*5 That in every thing ye are enriched by him, in all utterance, and in all knowledge;*

*6 Even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you:*

*7 So that ye come behind in no gift; waiting for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ:*

*8 Who shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.*

*9 God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.*

*10 Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.*

*11 For it hath been declared unto me of you, my brethren, by them which are of the house of Chloe, that there are contentions among you.*

*12 Now this I say, that every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ.*

*13 Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?*

*14 I thank God that I baptized none of you, but Crispus and Gaius;*

*15 Lest any should say that I had baptized in mine own name.*

*16 And I baptized also the household of Stephanas: besides, I know not whether I baptized any other.*

*17 For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect.*

*18 For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God.*

*19 For it is written, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent.*

*20 Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?*

*21 For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.*

*22 For the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom:*

*23 But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness;*

*24 But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God.*

*25 Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men.*

*26 For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called:*

*27 But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;*

*28 And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are:*

*29 That no flesh should glory in his presence.*

*30 But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption:*

*31 That, according as it is written, He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.*

Paul, as always begins with greetings, and as always, is writing to the saved believers in Christ. He had helped stablish this church in Corinth back in Acts 18, and so personally had led many of the church there to Christ. If you recall he was with Priscilla and Aquila there, and that they had also found a brother, baptized by John the Baptist, Apollos, to whom they introduced Jesus as the Christ, making his faith complete. This will be important to keep in mind as we read this epistle.

Paul greets them as saints, as are all who call upon the name of the Lord. Who are sanctified by Jesus.

And even as they were sanctified by the testimony of Christ, Paul expresses that God's grace continue to bless them in all things, so that they receive all spiritual gifts and knowledge and wisdom. This is the prayer we should have for ourselves and others in our church and those who share our faith. That by their faith, and God's grace they receive understanding and grow in their Christian life to be made more perfect, and in doing so become better use for God.

We see the promise of the coming of Christ, who will confirm us to the end, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, His second coming. The day of the resurrection and rapture. We are sealed unto judgment with a gift of eternal life that can never be lost or taken away. Jesus redeems us. God confirms us. The Spirit seals us. God is faithful.

After his greeting and the establishment or, re-establishment of the shared belief that unites those in Corinth, Paul gets to the heart of the matter in that he has heard reports of division in the church. Those who had been saved by Paul, or Apollos or Peter, and even those who had been saved during the ministry of Jesus Christ, are beginning to form schisms and divisions.

Paul is admonishing this, and points out that the baptism and who did it is incidental to the saving faith in Christ Jesus, in whose name they were baptized all. We see this a lot today, people treating what should be a unifying faith as a scene, and bickering about personalities within the scene. This is a real problem and, the denominational splits that we see in the church later all stem from it. Especially the schism that gives birth to the Roman Catholic Church 300 years later, and all of the devastation to Christianity that spun out of it.

Paul reminds them that the baptism isn't what they're there for, but to preach the gospel. Here Paul makes several doctrinal statements regarding the preaching of the Gospel that are both sublime truth, and yet obvious to those of us who are saved upon hearing it.

That the preaching of the Cross appears to be foolish to those who are either seeking after a sign from God, or to be reasoned with into faith. As Jesus said the only sign the Jews would receive was that of Jonas, of his being in the belly of the Earth for three days and three nights to be risen again. And for the greeks, who sought a reason above all, giving them faith which is the evidence of things unseen, in lieu of logic, appears to be foolishness.

We all know people today who are constantly looking for supernatural signs from God before they can commit to believing, or physical evidence of the truth of the Bible from secular sources. Or who seek to impose their own logic on matters that are spiritual. And who stuff at the simplicity of the Gospel as it's presented, despite our knowledge of the power of God that is within it.

Similar to the Epistle of James that we read over the weekend, Paul notes that the proud and wealthy, the powerful etc, are less likely to receive the Gospel because God uses our weaknesses to become our strength. Our humility and meekness becomes power in the hands of a believing Son of God. And what many see as foolishness, or weakness and passivity, or supposed slave mentality, is actually the wisdom of God expressed through our understanding, patience, long suffering, and the love that we show to all.

A lot of people grapple with this even saved Christians. They seek their own vengeance, they carry the wrath that belongs to God, they grow impatient with His perfect timing. For those who are not saved by faith, these things are a snare and a stumbling block, their pride being caught in those traps.

And Paul explains to us too that this all is in service of glory to God. That none of our works, or who we know, or any other ways that man might justify himself in his own wisdom and conceit, but that all we are and all our wisdom and knowledge, sanctification and redemption, comes from God himself and so all the glory goes to him.

There is a weird, Judaizing movement of Dispensationalists that has been very active online lately, teaching the cursed, damnable heresy that there are multiple Gospels, and that the Gospel given by Paul is different than that of Jesus or Peter.

It is wicked as Hell.

They use this beautiful rendition of the Gospel in **1 Corinthians 15**, which was received by Paul, to claim it is a different Gospel than what was testified by Peter. But a simple reading of the entire epistle puts this foolish notion to rest. They are ministers sharing the same good news, of the same risen Christ. As believed by Peter, the other Apostles, James, the 500 brethren, and Paul on the road to Damascus.

The same risen Christ that those in Corinth had believed on. There is no other foundation. *But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God. And the wisdom of God.*

*For we are laborers together.* Giving the same Gospel that Peter gave to the Gentile Cornelius and his house. That Paul preached in Corinth, where he *reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath, and persuaded the Jews and the Greeks.*

If you run into someone claiming to be a "1 Corinthians 15 Christian" gently correct them that all Christians, from Pentecost on, from Jerusalem and throughout the world, are "1 Corinthians 15 Christians," be they Jew or Gentile.

If they push back, rebuke. If they refuse. Shake the dust, they oppose themselves.
Here's one now.

The "Grace Movement," or Hyperdispensationalism, Bullingerism, etc, teaches a false gospel heresy that there's not only a difference between OT and NT salvation, Jews saved by works before Christ, and Gentiles by faith afterwards, but that there was a difference between the salvation taught in the Gospels, in the early  Acts, and the later Acts/Paul's epistles.

It was the late 19th/early 20th century creation of men like Bullinger in England and "J.C. O'Hair" in the U.S. and partially invented as a response to the rise of Pentecostalism in the 1800s, where the Pentecostalists insisted apostles and the gifts of the holy Ghost given to the first generation of the church continued in them.

But rather than simply debunking that by using the scriptures that define an apostle as a witness to the risen Christ, Bullingerians "discovered" a new doctrine, the "dispensation of the mystery" and that Paul's teaching of the death, burial and resurrection of Jesus was somehow different than the teaching of believing on the death, burial and resurrection of Jesus being taught to Jews by the Apostles, taught throughout Judea. To whom all the prophets gave witness. Which Jesus Himself charged the Apostles and disciples to preach to every creature.

It is a foolish and easily debunked heresy of a false gospel that requires one to "rightly divide the word" in a way that ignores Biblical accounts and clear scripture.

These false teachers claimed new revelation, that they'd been shown this truth by the Spirit, and that all of the Christians of that day who opposed them were in fact the false teachers, gate keeping this "hidden truth" from being discovered, of the "mystery" revealed to Paul.

My main understanding comes from interaction with its postalates, and searching scriptures to see if what they were saying was true.

It isn't, and so obviously false and another gospel, that it's almost impossible as a saved Christian to understand how they could believe what they do without being given over to strong delusion.

It also serves as a sort of mirror to the heresy of the "Hebrew Roots" movement that claims Christians should adopt OT laws and customs. Hyperdispensationalists teach, for example, that water baptism plays no part whatsoever in Christian tradition, after Paul received his "mystery."

It is also a strange cousin to those who deny Paul's writing, and say that the Apostle was a false prophet. That he taught a different gospel than Jesus, an equally absurd and easily exposed heresy. The Bullingerists and the Paul-deniers agree in principle, differing only in if he was of God or not.

**Galatians 3** plays a foundational role in this hyperdispensationalist "Grace movement," as it's the main source for their teaching that Paul had a new mystery revealed unto him by Jesus, and it was a different gospel for the Gentile. But that's not what this says at all, in fact, as God often does in His word, He presents the idea of an unknown, a mystery, a dark saying, and then provides the answer key to understanding it. God is not the author of confusion.

Here, in verse 6, we have the answer to the mystery Paul is talking about; that the Gentiles should be fellow heirs with the believing Jews. Partakers of the Fathers promise in Christ, by the Gospel. Partakers and heirs OF THE SAME BODY. By the same Gospel. And that Gospel is identical to the one given by Jesus in **John 3:16**. Salvation by grace through faith. Eternal life for all who believe on His name.

Further Paul expounds that this mystery, of Christ going to the Gentiles that all nations be blessed, was always the plan, from the foundation of the world, and as explained in **Galatians 3:8**;

*And the scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, preached before the gospel unto Abraham, saying, In thee shall all nations be blessed.*

**Genesis 22:18**
*and in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed; because thou hast obeyed my voice.*

**Romans 4:3**
*Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.*

**Genesis 15:6**
*And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness*.

The same Gospel. The same faith. Believing God's promise is true, being made righteous by His grace and the blood of His Son. In Whom all nations are blessed

Continuing the study of Spiritual Gifts, I want to refer to 1 Corinthians 12, which has the clearest writing on the topic, but first to establish the context of the epistle. Note Paul is writing at the request of a sister in Christ who reports that the church in Corinth has some troubles. Pride has set some brethren against others in respect to multiple issues.

The first being the source of their salvation, making it about the minister of the Gospel they received the word from, using the who as a way to puff themselves up. Paul and Apollos and Cephas camps, claiming a purer lineage in Christ. Of course Paul destroys this idea quickly. It isn't the minister, who sowed or watered or harvested, but the Lord who gains the increase.

And, as Paul says that his wish is the church at Corinth be of one mind in Christ, not filled with such divisions, because a church being united in the body of Christ is able to do great things for the Lord. But it can't if pride is giving way to error. Seeking our own glory, not glorying in the Lord.

Paul reminds them that God uses the weak, the seemingly foolish, to confound the wise and being to naught things that are, so that no flesh can glory in His presence.

Basically, to be humble and stop thinking you are a special boy. That not many wise men after the flesh, mighty men, nobles, are called. The wisdom of this world is not the wisdom of God.

And so it is in that spirit that Paul reminds them that they are there only in Christ, who God has made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption.

And so, Paul says if we are thankful for the grace of God given us in Christ, that in everything we are enriched by Him, in utterance and knowledge, which we already have seen is of the Spirit of God. And in that humility and understanding and gratitude, that even as the testimony of Christ is confirmed in us by that meek attitude, we shall *come behind in no gift*, meaning we can become more perfect or complete.

Second chapter of First Corinthians, Paul is still establishing a few things, making certain basic stipulations regarding the faith, before getting to his main topic of settling disputes that have come up in Corinth.

In chapter one, he speaks to the faith they share for salvation, and the fellowship of the sons of God that they should have in that faith and Spirit, given all wisdom and understanding come from God in that Spirit.

That unlike the Jews who ask for signs and evidence and the Greeks logic, but that God's wisdom comes from faith and meekness, that the strengths of this world are weakness, and our weakness, God's strength.

Paul continues this theme in chapter 2. Paul says he was determined when he came professing nothing of the world, but only Christ when evangelizing to them in the first place, and Him crucified. Reminding them he was with them as they heard and knew the truth and accepted it with fear.

Paul humbly says it wasn't his oratory or logic, but the power of the word that convicted them. That word is the "hidden wisdom" of Christ Jesus, written before creation. The reference to "mystery being revealed" isn't gnosticism, but that Jesus being the Christ, "to whom all the prophets gave witness" is the mystery revealed. Christianity is an anti-gnostic religion, in that knowledge of who Christ Jesus is and what He did and why is the great mystery that is told us plainly in the Gospel. It's the entry point to the full enlightenment for the novice, not some secret kept for the adept. Paul continues his teaching to the Church at Corinth, and reminds them all that their forefathers were baptized unto Moses by the passing through the sea, and by the cloud that followed them as they wandered, the Rock that provided water, a symbol of Christ. And despite this, those saved out of Egypt were backslidden and committed wickedness, as all sin common to man tempts us all.

They committed idolatry and idleness, with the golden calf (**Exodus 32**). They were tempted by the daughters of Moab and led to slaughter by their fornication (**Numbers 25)**. They complained of the Mana and were struck down by the fiery serpents (**Numbers 21**). They murmured and complained against Moses' leadership, and the gainsaying of Koreh was met with instant death (**Numbers 16)**.

These Israelites were faithful to leave captivity, made free by that faith, baptized of a sort, led to the promised land by a cloud and a pillar of fire, fed from the corn of Heaven, they did eat angel's food, and were given the water from the Rock, that was like the living waters of Christ. Paul says these examples are lessons given us by God to learn His ways. God will not allow us to be tempted beyond our ability to resist, but it is up to us to resist, by the path God provides us to escape each test and temptation.

That although we could do it, there are reasons why we shouldn't.

He draws the analogy between the communion of saints, the Lord's supper, symbolic act when we come together and bless the food we consume together in God's name, in remembrance of Jesus, we are like the levitical priests who partook in the sacrifice of the altars in the Old Testament. And where Christ died once for all men, the sole propitiation for our sin, we partake in the food and drink God has provided us in remembrance of him and that sacrifice.

And if we so partake, how does it look to other people whether they not be saved yet, or maybe babes in Christ, and they see us sit down at the table of idolatry to partake in those sacrifices?

And so we do not exercise our Liberty at the expense of others. We do not seek our own comfort and fortune, we should seek others. We should be pleasing to all men in service of the gospel. We should do without rather than offend.

This aspect of Christianity, that we are both free from all sin in the blood of Christ, and the knowledge that most things people think of as sin is a sin of the heart, because what goes into the mouth doesn't defile us, but what comes out. Because if what we do in our Liberty hampers another person's ability to believe or come to faith, or makes them struggle with the loss of their own flesh which turn to sin when exercised by them, then we must do without.

This is what Paul means by pleasing others. This is what loving your neighbor entails. We are to be weak to those who are weak that they might be strong.

I've gone into detail about the first half of this chapter before and made my opinion about the second half known even yesterday, but chapter 11 is one of contention for a lot of people.

The first half of the chapter, regarding "coverings" and shorn and shaven heads, is about hair and hair length.

Women are to have long hair, not cropped short. Men are to have short hair. It is a shame for a man to have long hair just as it is an abomination for him to wear that which pertainith to a woman.

We usually use the basic definition of charity to mean giving something away to help others, alms. And that certainly can be a form of expression for charity, but it is not itself charity as we see in verse 3.
